summary:
Erzurum province lies wholly inside Türkiye's national legal framework. No provincial regime applies to trans visitors: the penal code, the civil code, Health Ministry regulations and the police practices documented in Istanbul and Ankara operate identically in Erzurum.

Homosexuality has been decriminalised in Türkiye since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, the same year gender-reassignment surgery was legalised. That statutory position is the baseline a trans visitor enters on.

The trajectory runs the other way. A leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with penalties of up to three years, would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 under onerous eligibility conditions, and would allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care. The government's stated justification is protection of "the family" and "public morals". The package also carries unrelated measures including longer sentences for children and online-content removal.

Recognition is withheld across the board. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and joint adoption are not recognised, LGBTQ people are barred from openly serving in the military, and no comprehensive national law bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Türkiye 47th out of 49 countries.

Public assembly is the sharpest exposure point. Pride events have been banned in Istanbul and most other cities in most years since 2015, with police deploying tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants. A court case seeking to close the association Lambda Istanbul was overruled by the Constitutional Court, which kept the association open.
tangentialFactors:
The 11th Judicial Package is an omnibus instrument: its LGBT provisions travel alongside unrelated criminal-justice measures, including longer child sentences and online-content removal, which indicates the drafting is part of a wider legislative programme rather than an isolated provision.

İlga-Europe's 2026 ranking of 47th of 49 places Türkiye at the bottom tier of its regional comparison set, a useful cross-check against the country's own account of its legal protections.

Pride bans have applied since 2015 in Istanbul and most other cities, so the pattern of assembly restrictions predates the current draft legislation and is not dependent on it.
localsOnly:
Residents have been able to change legal gender since 1988, and gender-reassignment surgery has been legal in Türkiye since 1988; both facilities are part of the standing domestic regime, not a visitor accommodation.

Same-sex marriage, civil unions and joint adoption are not available to residents either, and LGBTQ people are barred from openly serving in the military.

No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so residents have no general statutory claim in employment, housing or services on those grounds.

The Constitutional Court's refusal to close Lambda Istanbul confirmed that associations may organise openly, subject to litigation risk.
